headline: I Am Now Responsible For Printing Birthday Cards From Global Leaders To The Prime Minister And It Is Destroying My Printer
body:
I work in the basement of the North Block as a Junior Administrative Assistant, a job that mostly involves unjamming the communal laserjet. However, ever since the trend of international leaders sending increasingly verbose birthday wishes to the Prime Minister began, my life has become a literal paper-fed nightmare. It is not just the sheer volume of high-gloss, gold-embossed PDF attachments from overseas heads of state; it is the fact that the protocol department insists these must be printed on 400 GSM cardstock, which my office printer was never designed to handle.

Yesterday, the machine caught fire attempting to render a 14-page congratulatory manifest from a leader who apparently thinks the PM is his pen pal. I spent four hours yesterday scraping melted toner off the rollers while my supervisor stood over me with a ruler, checking if the margins on the 'Dear Narendra' letter met international diplomatic standards. I have had to resort to using my own hairdryer to force-dry the ink on official stationery, just so the Prime Minister doesn't receive a smudged greeting from a foreign premier.

I’m currently hiding in the supply closet because I’ve run out of blue ink, and if I don't print the next batch of well-wishes from global powers within the next thirty minutes, I fear I might be the one replaced by an automated digital postcard system. My dreams are now exclusively about paper jams, and I wake up screaming whenever I hear the mechanical click-clack of a tray feeding paper. Please, to all the world's leaders: send an email, a text, or even a carrier pigeon—anything but another PDF that requires a industrial-grade printer to process.
caption: My printer has officially filed for divorce from my job description. Being the unofficial 'Birthday Greeting Coordinator' for international diplomacy is not for the faint of heart. #Diplomacy #OfficeLife #PaperJam #ModiBirthday #GovernmentWork (satire)

judgeVerdict.reasoning: Candidate 2 stands out by grounding the absurdity in a specific, relatable frustration: the physical limitations of an office printer. It avoids the repetitive 'I am now refusing to...' structure seen in other candidates, instead offering a vivid, frantic narrative that feels earned rather than formulaic.

safetyVerdict.reasoning: The piece uses a fictionalized scenario of an office worker dealing with excessive printer maintenance for birthday cards to create a satirical take on government bureaucracy. The mention of the Prime Minister is kept within the bounds of a harmless, whimsical, and absurd office-based premise, posing no risk of defamation or genuine reputation damage.
